raw_case_text:
A 42-year-old, otherwise healthy, male was admitted to the emergency room with a four-day history of malaise, myalgia, and high-grade fever. Laboratory tests showed increased liver enzymes (aspartate aminotransferase [AST] 2216 U/L and alanine aminotransferase [ALT] 1611 U/L), but normal bilirubin. Dengue Fever (DF) rapid test (NS1) and serology (ELISA IgM and IgG) were performed with negative results. Two days later the patient developed jaundice (total bilirubin 6.36 mg/dL and direct bilirubin 5.60 mg/dL) with a decrease in platelet count (52000 /mm3), normal international normalized ratio (INR) (0.85), and moderate proteinuria. At that time, abdominal ultrasonography showed hepatomegaly. Serology for viral hepatitis, Epstein-Barr virus, and Cytomegalovirus were negative. Dengue serology was repeated, and found positive, suggesting DF-related hepatitis. Despite an uncertain patient report of prior YF vaccination, YF polymerase chain reaction (YF-PCR) was performed considering the epidemiological risk and YF outbreak context. The patient was discharged after one week with improvement of laboratorial parameters (AST 259 U/L, ALT 638 U/L, alkaline phosphatase 153 U/L, platelets 294000 /mm3, and total bilirubin 2.25 mg/dL). The YF-PCR result was not available prior to discharge.
After 40 days, he was readmitted to the hospital with persistent fatigue, jaundice, and pruritus. Liver enzymes and bilirubin had increased (total bilirubin 19.2 mg/dL, AST 1037 U/L, ALT 2289 U/L, gamma-glutamyl transferase [GGT] 669 U/L, and INR 1.05). Extensive workup including serologies, ceruloplasmin, and ferritin was performed, but not indicative of a specific etiology. A hypothesis of autoimmune liver disorder was discarded by negative autoantibodies (i.e., anti-nuclear, anti-smooth muscle, and anti-mitochondria antibodies) and normal serum gamma-globulin. Liver biopsy demonstrated lobular hepatitis with mild neutrophilic infiltration (Figure 1). The remaining parenchymal cells showed frequent hepatocyte ballooning, macro- and microvacuolar steatosis, and rare apoptotic bodies. The patient was discharged again after a small decrease in total bilirubin without a definitive diagnosis. A follow-up hepatology appointment was scheduled for five days later. 
Upon hepatologist consultation, it was found that the YF-PCR ordered during the first hepatitis episode was positive, thus corroborating the suspicion of relapsing hepatitis due to YF. A pathological review was performed, including YF virus immunohistochemistry stain, but it was negative. The patient was started on ursodeoxycholic acid (10 mg/kg) and within three days improved his pruritus and bilirubin levels. In the two-week follow-up period, liver enzymes were normal, and the medication was suspended.

subjective.chief_complaint: A 42-year-old male presenting with a 4-day history of high-grade fever, malaise, and myalgia, followed by acute jaundice and a biphasic relapse of hepatitis 40 days later.
subjective.history_of_present_illness: The patient presented with 4 days of high fever, myalgia, and malaise, developing clinical jaundice 2 days into hospitalization. After initial clinical and biochemical improvement and discharge at 1 week, he was readmitted 40 days later with recurrent persistent fatigue, worsening jaundice, and generalized pruritus.
subjective.past_medical_history: Otherwise healthy 42-year-old male with uncertain prior yellow fever vaccination status during an active epidemiological yellow fever outbreak.
subjective.review_of_systems: Positive for fever, malaise, myalgia, persistent fatigue, jaundice, and pruritus.

objective.physical_examination: Initial presentation notable for high-grade fever and subsequent mucocutaneous jaundice (day 6); readmission at day 40 notable for marked jaundice and excoriations/pruritus.
objective.routine_investigations: Initial admission labs: AST 2,216 U/L, ALT 1,611 U/L, normal baseline bilirubin; 2 days later total bilirubin rose to 6.36 mg/dL (direct 5.60 mg/dL), platelets dropped to 52,000/mm3, INR 0.85, and urinalysis showed moderate proteinuria. Abdominal ultrasound showed hepatomegaly. Initial dengue NS1 and IgM/IgG ELISA, viral hepatitis panels, EBV, and CMV serologies were negative; repeat dengue serology was false-positive. At discharge (day 7): AST 259 U/L, ALT 638 U/L, ALP 153 U/L, platelets 294,000/mm3, total bilirubin 2.25 mg/dL. Readmission (day 40) labs: total bilirubin 19.2 mg/dL, AST 1,037 U/L, ALT 2,289 U/L, GGT 669 U/L, INR 1.05, with normal ceruloplasmin and ferritin.
objective.advanced_workup: Autoimmune hepatitis panel (ANA, anti-smooth muscle, anti-mitochondrial antibodies) and serum gamma-globulin levels were negative/normal. Percutaneous liver biopsy during readmission demonstrated lobular hepatitis with mild neutrophilic infiltration, hepatocyte ballooning, macro- and microvacuolar steatosis, and rare apoptotic bodies (negative YFV tissue immunohistochemistry).

assessment_and_plan.assessment_and_confirmation:
Definitive diagnosis: Confirmed biphasic/relapsing Yellow Fever hepatitis via positive serum Yellow Fever RT-PCR collected during the initial acute episode. Viral hepatitis, CMV, EBV, Wilson disease, and autoimmune hepatitis were ruled out.
Plan & Outcome: Managed supportively during the first admission and initiated on oral ursodeoxycholic acid (10 mg/kg/day) following outpatient hepatology review, achieving rapid resolution of pruritus and hyperbilirubinemia within 3 days and complete normalization of liver transaminases at 2-week follow-up.
